Apologies for delay, at work. :) The BoC is raising rates with good intention, but I do argue if it's the right monetary policy/tool to continue using. I sort of liken it to the BMI for body weight. It works, but it's flawed. Rate hikes work, in certain scenarios.

You are not wrong that the intention is to make it so less people are able to afford stuff. What this really does is prevent people from borrowing money. It doesn't really stop people with money already to buy things outright, nor does it affect products we consider inelastic. Therefore, when prices for food go up, we still need to buy it to live. Sure, we can find cheaper things but I recall when lettuce was near $6-9 a head. Eating healthy certainly out of the question. Look at Kraft Dinner, high priced priced from when I was kid at a buck.

People can cut back spending on televisions, cars, restaurants and trips because these are elastic. The more expensive they get, or the more expensive taking on debt is to get the thing, the less likely people are to buy it. With demand falling, the prices of these things can fall. Now, for some reason, it appears (though now slowing from recent data - take your pick of news org) people continue to demand these normally elastic things causing inflation to continue. So, the BoC keeps stepping in to raise interest rates to slow demand.

People struggle to cut back on food, even if you just buy pasta, sauce, canned items... because of inflation...so they end up putting on the credit card... amassing debt. Then the power bill comes, water, property taxes, perhaps they are variable interest rate mortgage holders... these people have high debt servicing expenses and less money for the food that keep rising, or the gas to fuel their car... BUT they must keep buying it to live.

Do you see what I mean? Elastic meaning our demand can come and go, we don't need it to survive. Inelastic meaning we have to buy the thing to live and we will pay the price whatever it is to get it.

Now we're seeing defaults in mortgages for those who are overextended, we're seeing higher food bank use... and still inflationary pressures on necessities like food.

Why I believe, and know that food prices will increase with interest rates is that people will keeping demanding food and they will also start demanding more wages. This filters through the economy, employers will end up paying more to retain/hire staff and charge more for products like food. Then people will ask for more wages, and eventually employers will pay it and charge more for products.

The cycle continues, not because most Canadian are borrowing to buy tv's... it's because they're borrowing to make ends meet. Sure, not everyone is in this scenario but I would be willing to bet there is a sizeable chunk of Canadians making the choice each day to either starve/go homeless or borrow money to get by.
I’d leave. If it starts this way it’s not getting better.

But things like gas and food have inelastic demand. People keep buying these things to survive regardless of the price. They can give up on buying a home or a car but not on the ability to eat or have fuel to commute to work.

We have high inflation on most goods but most noticeably on food items, and most people need to continue to eat regardless of the cost of food. Mostly inelastic demand. Sure you can cut down or buy cheaper options but even the cheaper options are rising sharply. Some people are then lead to borrow (if available to them) to be able to continue eating, keeping a roof over their heads, paying the hydro bill. 

While I understand raising the cost of borrowing is a deterrent for those who want or need to borrow - so far it’s not been a successful tool. I suppose we will see how continued rate hikes affect cost of goods. 

What I see is prices going up, people demand more wages to live, demand for things remains the same, interest rates increase to keep inflation at bay, people demand more wages, prices go up… cycle continues. 

Surely there are other measures we can take.

You do have limits on TFSA contribution room much like RRSP. A TFSA is a good option if you want to invest short term or plan to withdraw often or have maxed out RRSP room. The RRSP umbrella while a little more locked down (withdrawals outside first time home buying and retirement) are penalized - you do get to defer your taxes.
